title: Composition, and when not to make a module
summary: Root modules that compose small modules, passing outputs between them, providers and aliases into modules, the module that does not have the output you need, and the modules that should not exist.

steps.title: Compose small modules in the root
body: Good Terraform repos keep modules **small and flat**, and let the root module wire them together:
subnet_ids = module.network.private_subnet_ids   # one module's output is another's input
providers = { aws = aws.us_east_1 }             # CloudFront certificates must live in us-east-1
Modules that call modules that call modules are hard to read and to upgrade. Pass **data in** (IDs, names), not
whole objects, and give every output a description: an output is a public interface, removing or renaming one is
a breaking change for every caller.

steps.title: The output that is not there
prompt: The load balancer team added two things to `~/infra/web/main.tf`: a file with the shop's certificate and an output
with its fingerprint. `terraform plan` fails. Read the error: which object, which attribute? Fix it where it belongs
(the module should offer it, with a description), then plan and apply.

checks.name: the module offers cert_fingerprint
checks.cmd: cd ~/infra/web && grep -q 'output "cert_fingerprint"' modules/site/*.tf && grep -A3 'output "cert_fingerprint"' modules/site/*.tf | grep -q description

checks.name: the LB has the certificate
checks.cmd: cd ~/infra/web && grep -q 'BEGIN CERTIFICATE' out/lb/shop.example.com.pem && terraform plan -detailed-exitcode -input=false -no-color >/dev/null
checks.fail: Apply, so `out/lb/shop.example.com.pem` exists and `terraform plan` shows no changes.

hints: *Unsupported attribute: This object does not have an attribute named "cert_fingerprint"* on `module.shop`: a module only exposes its outputs.
Then `terraform plan -out=tfplan` and `terraform apply tfplan`. No `init` is needed: the module's source did not change.
steps.explain: Callers can only see what a module outputs; there is no reaching inside (`module.shop.tls_private_key.site` is not a valid expression). For a shared module in its own repo, the same fix is a new minor version: adding an output is backwards compatible, removing one is not.

steps.prompt: Make it a module, or not?
items: a service's standard stack (bucket, queue, alarms) that six teams deploy
a wrapper around `aws_s3_bucket` that passes every argument straight through
a network layout with the company's subnet and routing rules
one resource used once, "in case we need it again"
a module that takes `var.config` (an `any` map) and decides everything inside
a certificate plus its DNS validation records, always used together
steps.explain: A module earns its place by encoding a decision (a standard, a pattern used together, a policy) behind a small, typed interface. Thin pass-through wrappers add a version to upgrade and hide nothing; `any`-typed mega-modules hide everything, including bugs.

steps.prompt: A module needs resources in two AWS regions (a certificate in `us-east-1` for CloudFront, everything else in `eu-west-1`). How does it get both providers?
options: It declares `configuration_aliases = [aws.us_east_1]` in `required_providers`, and the caller passes `providers = { aws = aws, aws.us_east_1 = aws.virginia }`
It writes two `provider "aws"` blocks inside the module
The caller runs it twice with `-target`, once per region
It cannot: a module only gets one provider
steps.explain: Providers are configured in the root and passed in. A module that needs an extra, aliased provider says so with `configuration_aliases`; its resources pick it with `provider = aws.us_east_1`. (The AWS provider 6.x also lets most resources take a `region` argument directly, which removes many aliases, but the alias pattern is everywhere in existing code and in other providers.)
